title: The heavens torn open (Mark 1:9–13)
hookLine: the sky rips, the Spirit comes down like a dove, then straight into the desert
last: THE BEGINNING OF THE GOOD NEWS.

cards: John said someone mightier was coming. Now he arrives, and Mark gives him no introduction at all. No backstory, no childhood.
Just: in those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan. One sentence. He walks down into the river with everyone else.
Then he comes up out of the water, and Mark describes what happens with a word so violent it's almost shocking. Not the sky opening politely, like curtains. The sky ripping.
And before you've even caught your breath, it's over, and he's alone in the desert. Five verses.

teach.b: The King James Bible says it gently: "And straightway coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens opened, and the Spirit like a dove descending upon him." But Mark's Greek word is schizō: to tear, to split, to rip.
It's the root of the English word schism. Matthew and Luke, telling the same scene, use the ordinary word for open. Mark says torn.

teach.h: TORN AT THE START, TORN AT THE CROSS.
teach.b: And the verb comes back at the very end of Mark: when Jesus dies on the cross, the curtain of the Temple is torn in two from top to bottom.
Same word, beginning and end, framing the whole story: heaven ripped open to earth. Then a voice: "Thou art my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Notice when it comes.
Before a single miracle. Before a sermon.
Before he's done anything at all. Beloved first.

Then, right away, the turn: "And immediately the spirit driveth him into the wilderness." Driveth is a strong word, the one Mark later uses for casting out demons. The Spirit that came down like a dove now drives him out.

Forty days in the wilderness, tempted by Satan, with the wild beasts, and angels serving him. Mark gives none of the conversation with the tempter that Matthew and Luke tell. Just wild animals and angels, side by side.
Some readers take comfort from the order: being beloved doesn't mean skipping the desert. In Mark, the voice comes first.

how: Many churches remember Jesus's baptism at the feast of the Baptism of the Lord or Theophany in January, and some lectionaries read Mark's desert verses at the start of Lent, when a season of forty days begins.

o: to tear or rip apart, like the sky at his baptism
to shine brightly with light from heaven
to open gently, like curtains pulled aside

games.q: what's inside the passage — tap the pairs.

s: Mark says the heavens opened gently
Mark's word is schizō, torn. Matthew and Luke say opened.
Mark uses the same word when the Temple curtain tears
torn at the start, torn at the cross.
Mark describes the conversation with Satan in the desert
Mark gives no dialogue, just forty days, Satan, wild beasts and angels.

games.q: the voice from heaven has just said: thou art my beloved Son. what happens next in Mark?
o: the Spirit immediately drives him into the wilderness.
he goes home to Nazareth to rest.
games.why: "and immediately the spirit driveth him into the wilderness." beloved first, then the desert.

practice: Slow Mark down: picture the water, then coming up out of it.
If you're a Christian, you might hear the voice as spoken to you too, through baptism: beloved; if you're not, simply notice what it would mean to be loved before you've done anything.
Then think about the desert you're walking into this week, and let the first word go with you into it.

wordCard.voice: Schizō, Mark's violent word for tear or rip: the heavens torn open at his baptism, and the Temple curtain torn at his death.

orig.note: Greek: being torn apart — Mark's word for the heavens (1:10); schism comes from the same root.

carryVoice: Your line: beloved, then the desert. The dove and the driving come from the same Spirit. Day one hundred fifty-eight, done.
